body:
Why wind deposits sediment

Wind deposits its transported sediment when its ability to carry particles decreases. A reduction in wind speed, changes in surface conditions and obstacles such as vegetation can encourage deposition.

Relatively coarse sand generally settles sooner than fine airborne dust. Sand accumulates in dunes, whereas fine windblown silt can form extensive loess deposits.

Both the Thar Desert of northwestern India and large deserts such as the Sahara contain extensive landscapes shaped by windblown sand.

Structure and migration of a sand dune

A sand dune is a mound or ridge of loose sand accumulated by wind. Dunes develop where a sufficient sand supply is available and the wind can transport and redeposit it.

A typical migrating dune formed under a dominant wind direction possesses a relatively gentle windward slope and a steeper leeward slope, also called the slip face.

Sand grains move up the windward slope through saltation and creep. When sand accumulates beyond the crest, it can slide down the leeward slope under gravity. Repetition of this process causes the dune to migrate downwind.

Major types of sand dunes

Barchan dunes

Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes that typically develop where a dominant wind blows over a surface with limited sand and little vegetation. Their 2 horns extend downwind. The central slip face is generally located on the leeward side.

Parabolic dunes

Parabolic dunes are U-shaped or crescent-shaped dunes commonly associated with partially vegetated sandy surfaces. Vegetation anchors the arms, while the central portion moves downwind. Their arms extend upwind, opposite to those of barchans.

Parabolic dunes are common in some coastal and semi-arid environments.

Transverse dunes

Transverse dunes form extensive ridges with crests approximately perpendicular to the prevailing wind direction. They commonly develop where the sand supply is relatively abundant and winds blow predominantly from one direction.

Longitudinal or linear dunes

Longitudinal dunes are elongated sand ridges extending broadly parallel to the resultant direction of sand transport. They may develop under persistent winds or under winds approaching from 2 dominant oblique directions. Seif dunes are a recognised type of elongated linear dune.

Star dunes

Star dunes are large, pyramidal accumulations of sand with several ridges extending outward from a central summit. They develop under complex, multidirectional wind conditions.

The most important dune distinction

Barchan horns point downwind. Parabolic dune arms point upwind. Transverse crests lie across the prevailing wind, while longitudinal dunes generally extend along the resultant direction of sand transport.

Loess deposits

Loess is an extensive deposit of predominantly silt-sized material transported and deposited by wind. Unlike a sand dune, loess typically forms widespread blankets rather than individual accumulations of coarse sand.

Loess may originate from desert dust, exposed floodplain sediment or finely ground material produced by glaciers. Glacial abrasion can create rock flour, which meltwater deposits on exposed surfaces. Wind may subsequently transport this material and deposit it as loess.

The Loess Plateau of northern China, associated with the Huang He or Yellow River basin, is a prominent example of extensive loess accumulation.

Loess commonly develops productive agricultural soils because it consists of fine mineral particles and can retain water. However, exposed loess is highly susceptible to erosion, particularly by running water, which may produce deep gullies.

Prelims focus

  • A typical migrating dune has a gentle windward slope and a steeper leeward slip face.
  • Barchan horns point downwind; parabolic dune arms point upwind.
  • Transverse dunes extend across the prevailing wind direction.
  • Star dunes indicate multidirectional wind conditions.
  • Loess is predominantly wind-deposited silt; northern China contains extensive loess deposits.
  • Trap: Loess need not originate exclusively from deserts; glacially produced rock flour is also a possible source.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 3, Work of Wind; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, Sand Dunes and Figure 7.16, online copy; U.S. National Park Service, Dune Types and Monitoring Aeolian Features and Processes; U.S. Geological Survey, Geology of Great Sand Dunes National Park and Eolian Sediments, 2 December 2020; consulted 28 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of desertification

Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry subhumid areas resulting from various factors, including climatic variations and human activities.

This definition is established under Article 1 of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD).

Desertification reduces the biological or economic productivity of dryland ecosystems. It does not necessarily result in the formation of a sandy desert. Degraded land may instead become eroded, compacted, saline or sparsely vegetated.

Desertification, drought and natural deserts

TermMeaning
DesertA naturally arid environment characterised by very limited precipitation
DroughtA period of unusually deficient precipitation and associated water shortage
DesertificationDegradation of land productivity in dryland environments

A drought can contribute to desertification by reducing vegetation and soil moisture. However, drought is a climatic condition, whereas desertification involves degradation of the land itself. Natural deserts are not necessarily degraded ecosystems.

Principal causes

Climatic factors

  • Prolonged or recurrent drought reduces vegetation cover.
  • High evaporation and limited rainfall restrict the recovery of vegetation and soil moisture.
  • Strong winds can remove exposed soil and redistribute sand.
  • Intense rainfall on bare or degraded ground may produce severe water erosion.

Human activities

  • Overgrazing: Excessive removal of vegetation exposes soil to erosion and reduces plant regeneration.
  • Deforestation: Removal of trees and shrubs reduces soil protection and weakens the stabilisation of sediments.
  • Unsustainable cultivation: Repeated cultivation without adequate soil protection can reduce organic matter and accelerate erosion.
  • Poor irrigation and drainage: Waterlogging and evaporation can cause soluble salts to accumulate in the root zone, reducing agricultural productivity.
  • Excessive groundwater extraction: Declining groundwater availability can increase water stress and undermine the sustainability of dryland agriculture.

Consequences of desertification

Loss of fertile topsoil reduces agricultural productivity and the water-holding capacity of soil. Increased sediment movement may bury crops, damage roads and generate dust storms. Deterioration of grazing resources affects livestock-dependent livelihoods.

Desertification can become self-reinforcing. Vegetation loss exposes soil to erosion, and erosion removes nutrients and reduces moisture retention. These changes make vegetation recovery more difficult.

Measures to reduce desertification

MeasurePurpose
Shelterbelts and windbreaksReduce wind speed and soil erosion
Strip croppingInterrupt wind movement across exposed fields
Mulching and ground coverProtect soil and conserve moisture
Controlled grazingAllow vegetation and grasslands to regenerate
Sand dune stabilisationReduce movement of loose sand using suitable vegetation
Efficient irrigation and drainageReduce water wastage, waterlogging and salinisation
Rainwater harvestingImprove water availability and support vegetation recovery

Shelterbelts are rows of trees or shrubs planted to reduce wind velocity. They are especially effective when oriented across the prevailing erosive winds. Native and drought-tolerant species are generally preferable in dryland restoration because they are adapted to local climatic conditions.

Dryland environments in Gujarat

Kachchh and parts of northern Gujarat contain extensive dryland environments where wind erosion, water scarcity and soil salinity are important land-management concerns.

Windblown sediment also contributes to the geological deposits of the Gujarat plains. These deposits should be distinguished from alluvium transported by running water.

The Space Applications Centre of ISRO, located in Ahmedabad, uses satellite-based observations to map desertification and land degradation. Remote sensing helps identify the extent, distribution and changes of degraded land, including areas affected by wind erosion and salinisation.

Prelims focus

  • UNCCD Article 1 includes arid, semi-arid and dry subhumid regions in the definition of desertification.
  • Both climatic variations and human activities can cause desertification.
  • Salinisation can degrade agricultural land without forming sand dunes.
  • Shelterbelts reduce wind velocity and protect exposed soil.
  • Space Applications Centre, ISRO, Ahmedabad, undertakes desertification and land degradation mapping.
  • Trap: Desertification is not simply the geographical expansion of existing natural deserts.

[References: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, 2018–19, Chapter 2, Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources; United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, Article 1; Space Applications Centre, ISRO, Desertification Status Mapping Atlas portal; Central Ground Water Board and Government of Gujarat, Report on Dynamic Ground Water Resources of Gujarat State 2024, December 2024, Section 3.6.5; online sources consulted 28 November 2026.]

title: Desertification: Causes, Effects and Dryland Conservation

body:
Meaning and development of karst

Karst is a distinctive landscape produced primarily by the chemical dissolution of soluble rocks. It is most commonly associated with limestone and dolomite, although similar landscapes may develop in other soluble rocks, including gypsum and rock salt.

The term karst originates from the limestone region near the Adriatic Sea in the Balkans. Karst landscapes are characterised by solution depressions, fissures, caves, underground drainage and mineral deposits.

Chemical dissolution of limestone

Limestone consists predominantly of calcium carbonate, represented by CaCO3. Pure water dissolves calcium carbonate only to a limited extent, but natural rainwater and groundwater often contain dissolved carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide enters water from the atmosphere and, commonly in greater concentrations, from biological activity in the soil. It combines with water to form weak carbonic acid, represented by H2CO3.

Carbonic acid reacts with calcium carbonate, producing dissolved calcium and bicarbonate. This is commonly represented in simplified form as the formation of soluble calcium bicarbonate, Ca(HCO3)2.

Water carrying the dissolved material moves away through the rock. Continued dissolution gradually enlarges fractures and produces underground passages and surface depressions.

Conditions favourable for karst development

  • Availability of soluble rock, particularly extensive limestone or dolomite formations.
  • Joints, fractures and bedding planes that permit water to enter and circulate through the rock.
  • Sufficient rainfall or other water supply to sustain dissolution.
  • Carbon dioxide in the water, which increases its ability to dissolve carbonate minerals.
  • Conditions that allow dissolved material to be transported away.

Karst development is not confined to tropical or humid regions. It can occur under different climatic conditions wherever suitable soluble rocks and water are available, although climate influences the intensity and nature of dissolution.

Surface erosional landforms

Lapies or karren

Lapies are small grooves, channels and sharp ridges produced by solution on exposed limestone surfaces. Water preferentially dissolves the rock along cracks and depressions, creating an irregular surface.

A limestone pavement may consist of relatively flat limestone blocks called clints separated by widened solution fissures called grikes.

Sinkhole or doline

A sinkhole is a closed depression formed when soluble rock is dissolved or when the ground subsides or collapses into an underground cavity. Sinkholes vary from shallow depressions to deep, steep-sided openings.

A doline is a characteristic closed depression of a karst landscape. Sinkholes may form gradually through surface solution or suddenly when the roof of an underground cavity fails.

Swallow hole

A swallow hole is an opening through which surface water, particularly a stream, enters the underground drainage system. Some sinkholes function as swallow holes, but not every sinkhole carries a surface stream.

Uvala

When neighbouring dolines enlarge and merge, they may produce a larger, irregular depression called an uvala.

Polje

A polje is a large, enclosed karst depression with a relatively flat floor and steep surrounding slopes. Drainage may occur through underground openings. Some poljes experience seasonal flooding when inflowing water exceeds the capacity of their underground outlets.

Tower karst

In some humid tropical and subtropical limestone regions, prolonged dissolution and erosion leave isolated steep-sided limestone hills above relatively low surrounding land. Such landscapes are known as tower karst. The limestone landscapes of southern China provide well-known examples.

Prelims focus

  • Limestone solution is a chemical process involving carbon dioxide-rich water.
  • Calcium carbonate is converted into dissolved calcium and bicarbonate.
  • Lapies are solution grooves; clints and grikes are features of limestone pavements.
  • Dolines are closed depressions; uvalas may develop through their merger.
  • A polje is a large, relatively flat-floored karst depression.
  • Trap: Karst is not restricted exclusively to limestone or to humid tropical climates.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, Groundwater and Erosional Landforms, printed pp. 65–66 and Figure 7.10, online copy; U.S. Geological Survey, Karst Aquifers, What Is a Sinkhole? and Carbonate-Rock Aquifers; consulted 28 November 2026.]
